title: Darjeeling Food: Momos, Thukpa, Sel Roti and Tea
meta_description: What to eat in Darjeeling: momos, thukpa, thenthuk, shaphaley, sel roti, gundruk, kinema and chhurpi, how to taste first and second flush tea, and prices.
summary: Darjeeling food is Tibetan, Nepali and old hill-station British on one ridge. Eat momos, thukpa and thenthuk in the market lanes, sel roti at festivals, gundruk, kinema and chhurpi in homes and thali kitchens, and taste first and second flush tea without milk. A good day of eating costs ₹450–1,000.

sections.heading: What Darjeeling eats
paras: Darjeeling's kitchen is the story of the hills on a plate. Tibetan families brought momos, thukpa and butter tea; Nepali households brought dal-bhat, fermented greens, sel roti and fiery pickles; the Lepcha and Limbu added their own fermented foods; and the British left bakeries, sausages and the afternoon pot of tea. Most families cook all of it at some point in the week.

For a visitor that means two kinds of eating. In the market lanes below Chowrasta and around Chowk Bazaar you find steaming momo counters, thukpa bowls and thali kitchens at working-people prices. In homestays and village kitchens you meet the slower foods that rarely appear on menus: gundruk soup, kinema curry, chhurpi pickle and squash shoots from the garden. Ask your host what they are eating tonight; it is usually better than anything on the menu. Breakfast in the hills is often puri or roti with aloo dum, or bread and eggs, with sweet milky tea.

sections.heading: Momos, thukpa and thenthuk
paras: Momos are steamed dumplings of Tibetan origin, folded around minced pork, chicken, beef or cabbage and cheese, and served with a thin clear soup and a red chilli and tomato chutney. A plate of eight to ten costs ₹80–150. Fried and pan-fried versions exist, but steamed is the test of a kitchen: the wrapper should be thin and the filling juicy. Eat them at lunchtime when the steamers are freshest.

Thukpa is the noodle soup that keeps the hills warm: round noodles in broth with vegetables, egg or meat, ₹100–180 a bowl. Thenthuk is its cousin, with flat hand-pulled noodle pieces torn straight into the pot, thicker and more filling, and our choice on a wet afternoon. Many Tibetan kitchens also make laphing, a cold, spicy mung-bean noodle dish sold from street stalls in summer.

sections.heading: Shaphaley, sel roti and festival food
paras: Shaphaley (also spelled shapale) is a Tibetan fried bread, a round or half-moon of dough stuffed with spiced minced meat and cabbage, crisp outside and soft inside. It is a snack and a meal at once, and best straight from the oil with a cup of tea.

Sel roti is the Nepali ring-shaped bread made from a batter of ground rice, sugar and ghee or butter, poured by hand in a circle into hot oil. It is sweet, crisp at the edges and slightly chewy, and it is the taste of Dashain and especially Tihar, when every kitchen fries stacks of it to share with neighbours and visitors. Outside festivals you can buy it in the market in the mornings, often eaten with aloo dum, the hills' spiced potato curry, or with tea.

sections.heading: Gundruk, kinema and chhurpi
paras: The fermented foods are what make hill cooking different from anything on the plains, and they are worth seeking out.
list: Gundruk: leaves of mustard, radish or cauliflower, wilted, packed tight to ferment and then sun-dried. It turns up as a sour, warming soup, cooked with potatoes or soybeans, or as a pickle. Families make it in winter when greens are plentiful.

Kinema: soybeans boiled, wrapped and fermented for a few days until sticky and strong-smelling, then cooked as a curry with onion, tomato and chilli. It is associated especially with the Limbu and other Kirat communities and is an acquired taste we have come to love.
Soft chhurpi: a fresh cheese made from buttermilk, mild and crumbly, mixed into chhurpi ko achar, a pickle with chilli and tomato, or cooked with greens and fiddlehead fern (ningro) in season.

Hard churpi: the same cheese pressed, dried and smoked until it is as hard as stone. You do not bite it, you hold a cube in your cheek and chew slowly for an hour or more. Shops sell it in small packets; it travels well as a gift.

sections.heading: Tasting Darjeeling tea properly
paras: Darjeeling tea is grown in about 87 gardens and was India's first product to receive a Geographical Indication tag, in 2004. Genuine Darjeeling carries the Tea Board's Darjeeling logo; cheap packets sold as Darjeeling are often blends. Drink it the way the gardens taste it: no milk, no sugar, so you can tell one flush from another.

First flush is picked from about March into April, after winter. The liquor is pale gold, light and floral, with a fresh, slightly brisk finish; it is the most prized and the most expensive. Second flush, in May and June, is amber and fuller, with the ripe-fruit taste called muscatel that made Darjeeling famous. Monsoon flush is stronger and cheaper, used mostly in blends, and autumn flush in October and November is mellow and coppery.

To taste at home or in a tea room, use about 2–3 g of leaf for a 150–200 ml cup, with water just off the boil, slightly cooler for first flush, and steep for three to four minutes. Look at the dry leaf, the colour of the cup and the wet leaf, then smell before you sip. Grades such as FTGFOP describe leaf size and tips, not taste, so trust your tongue more than the label.

sections.heading: Glenary's, Keventer's and the tea rooms
paras: Two long-running institutions are part of the Darjeeling routine for many families. Glenary's on Nehru Road is a bakery and café with cakes, breads and pastries downstairs and a restaurant above with wide windows over the valley. Keventer's at Clubside is known for its breakfast terrace: ham, sausages, eggs and hot chocolate in the morning sun, looking over the rooftops. Both cost more than the market lanes; we treat them as a once-per-trip breakfast or tea rather than daily meals.

Around the Mall and Chowrasta you will find tea rooms and tea shops where you can order a pot of a named garden's first or second flush for ₹40–150. Ask to compare two flushes side by side. A good shop will let you smell the leaf before you buy, and will tell you the garden and the picking.

sections.heading: Eating well for less, and what to take home
paras: Food is the easiest part of a Darjeeling budget to keep in check, because the cheapest food is also the most local. Make lunch your main meal, eat where people are queuing, and leave the café menus for one breakfast. In homestays, dinner and breakfast are usually included, and the home cooking is often the best food of the trip.

For the journey home, the hills give you food that travels. Pack a few things in your hand luggage rather than buying at the station, where choice is thin and prices are higher. Sealed packs travel best in a checked bag.
list: Loose-leaf tea from a named garden, first flush for a gift and second flush for daily drinking, in sealed packs.
Hard churpi in small packets, which keeps for months.
Dried gundruk, if you have a kitchen and a sense of adventure.
Bakery biscuits or a fruit cake from one of the old bakeries for the train.
A jar of local chilli pickle, sealed tight, for those who like heat.

sections.heading: What food costs in Darjeeling
paras: Indicative prices for 2025–26 in ordinary local places; cafés around Chowrasta and the Mall charge more. A shoestring day of eating costs ₹450–700, and a comfortable day with a café breakfast and a sit-down dinner about ₹700–1,000.

faqs.q: What food is Darjeeling famous for?
faqs.a: Momos and thukpa are the everyday favourites, alongside Darjeeling tea. Look also for thenthuk, shaphaley, sel roti, aloo dum, gundruk soup, kinema curry and chhurpi pickle, which show the Tibetan and Nepali roots of hill cooking. The old British bakeries and breakfast terraces, such as Glenary's and Keventer's, are part of the food story too.

faqs.q: Where can I eat good momos in Darjeeling?
faqs.a: In the market lanes below Chowrasta and around Chowk Bazaar, and in the small Tibetan kitchens on the roads off the Mall. Choose a busy counter with steam rising and locals eating, and go at lunchtime when batches are freshest. A plate costs about ₹80–150. We do not name single stalls, because small kitchens open and close often.

faqs.q: What is the difference between first flush and second flush Darjeeling tea?
faqs.a: First flush is picked from about March into April. It is pale gold, light and floral, with a brisk finish, and fetches the highest prices. Second flush follows in May and June, and is amber and fuller, with the ripe-fruit muscatel character Darjeeling is famous for. Taste both without milk to notice the difference.

faqs.q: What is chhurpi, and how do you eat it?
faqs.a: Chhurpi is a cheese of the Himalayan hills. Soft chhurpi is a fresh, crumbly cheese made from buttermilk and used in pickles and curries. Hard churpi is the same cheese pressed, dried and smoked until stone-hard; you hold a cube in your mouth and chew it slowly for an hour or more. Small packets make a good gift.

The dishes themselves are usually mild. The heat comes from the chutneys and pickles served on the side, especially those made with the small round local chilli, which is very hot. Ask for chutney separately if you are not used to chilli. Momos, thukpa and thenthuk are gentle enough for most children and older travellers.

faqs.q: Is it easy to find vegetarian food in Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Yes. Most momo counters offer veg momos with cabbage, carrot or cheese, thali kitchens serve full vegetarian thalis for ₹150–250, and thukpa comes in vegetable versions. Gundruk soup, aloo dum and sel roti are vegetarian too. Strict vegetarians should ask about broth, since some soups use a meat stock even for vegetable dishes.

Sel roti is a Nepali ring-shaped bread made from a batter of ground rice, sugar and ghee or butter, poured by hand into hot oil. It is sweet, crisp outside and slightly chewy inside. Families fry large batches at Dashain and especially Tihar, and you can buy it from morning market stalls for about ₹20–40 a piece.

faqs.q: Are Glenary's and Keventer's worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, once. Glenary's on Nehru Road is a bakery and café with a restaurant upstairs looking over the valley, and Keventer's at Clubside is known for its breakfast terrace with sausages, ham and hot chocolate. Both cost more than the market lanes, so we treat them as a single treat breakfast or tea in a trip.

faqs.q: How do I make sure I am buying real Darjeeling tea?
faqs.a: Look for the Tea Board's Darjeeling logo and the name of a garden and flush on the pack, and buy from a shop that lets you smell or taste before you pay. Very cheap packets labelled Darjeeling are often blends. Expect to pay noticeably more for a named first flush than for a monsoon or autumn tea.
